GenAI-using developers say they mostly employ it for 'research and brainstorming'
A recent survey clocked AI-generated coding as the third-most common use case for industry professionals employing generative AI.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 12, 2026
schedule
3 Min Read
Image by Siarhei via Adobe Stock.
What purpose does generative AI serve in game development?
That question is one developers have sought to answer since generative AI technology came onto the scene and started popping up in every tool, platform, and service with the commercial advent of large language models (LLMs) in 2022. Recently, the role of generative AI in coding has
risen to the top of many of these discussions
, but new data from the
GDC Festival of Gaming State of the Game Industry report
indicates that's not the number one use among industry professionals.
According to the report, 40 percent of industry professionals use generative AI in the workplace. Of those, 73 percent of respondants marked that "research/brainstorming" was their number one use case. 62 percent said they used it for "data analysis and summarization" and only 56 percent said they use it for "code generation/debugging." Respondents were allowed to select multiple options that described their use of the tool.

That indicates that in the world of professional game development, only half of generative AI users are using the technology to generate code.
Meanwhile 37 percent of respondents said they use the technology for game prototyping. 22 percent said they use it for "concept art and visual ideation." While some respondents said they use generative ai for content personalization or procedural generation, ultimately only six percent of player said they use the technology to create what will eventually become "player-facing content"
What forces are shaping the use of generative AI?
Adoption of generative AI tooling has been met
with exceptionally fierce resistance
by
segments
of the professional game development community, with previous data indicating that half of developers are worried that the tech may
lower the quality of games
. Throughout both this year's survey and reports from prior years, respondents explaining their feelings about generative AI also remain concerned over the environmental impact of AI tools and the use of copywritten material in their foundational training data.
The survey also captures sentiment from developers who say generative AI tech has enhanced their programming capabilities. This is similar to earlier comments from experts programmers like
DayZ
creator and Rocketwerkz creator Dean Hall
have explained
the tool has accelerated their ability to make games using complex programming languages and frameworks. This isn't done through "vibe coding," a practice of progressively prompting AI to make software features, but rather taking advantage of LLMs' capability to "tokenize language."
Related:
Zelda producer: Ocarina of Time remake helps junior staff learn classic insights
The use of generative AI to make in-game audio/visual assets or other content has been a particularly risky landmine for studios, who often have had to
backpedal
or
alter course
after unveiling said content to players.
This data from the latest edition of the State of the Game Industry report highlights how vastly adoption of and use cases for generative AI technology can vary from role to role and studio to studio. From the outside looking in, generative AI is proselytized as a tool capable of
generating entire games
,
replacing artists
, and
creating fully-simulated non-playable characters
, and
generating entire games
.
And yet the data also indicates that for game developers across many markets, disciplines, a rather different use case has started to form.
